h1:
Surin Elephant Festival November Plan
Stay, Parking, and Catching the Show on Time
intro: The Surin Elephant Festival is the busiest time of year in town: hotels fill up fast, the central streets close in sections, and each highlight happens on a different day at a different time. Show up without a plan and you can easily miss the arena show, which only runs on Saturday and Sunday. So this is a 2-day, 1-night plan built to catch the Friday elephant buffet, the Saturday arena show, and the elephant fair at night, with honest notes on parking, shuttle trams, and what you should book ahead of time.

blocks.html: The Surin Elephant Festival, officially called the Surin Elephant Round-up, runs in mid-November every year and stretches over about two weeks. The most recent edition (2025) ran from 15 to 26 November, and the province has set the 2026 dates at roughly 14 to 25 November. The event has two parts: the market side, known as the elephant fair, which is open every day throughout, and the elephant show in the arena, which only runs on a handful of days. The tricky thing about this festival is that the highlights are spread across different days, so if you don't line up your schedule well you'll only catch part of it.

The key to planning is to anchor on three days in a row: Friday, Saturday, Sunday in the middle of the festival. Friday is usually the day of the elephant buffet (feeding the elephants in the town center), and the weekend is when the show runs in the big arena. If you only have one weekend, this plan helps you catch all three without rushing yourself into exhaustion.

blocks.text: First, confirm the dates before you book anything

blocks.html: The festival dates shift year to year, and the actual arena show days may not line up with the first day of the festival. The things you need to lock down before booking transport or a hotel are the arena show days and the elephant buffet day. The pattern is usually the same every year: the elephant buffet on Friday morning, and the arena show on Saturday and Sunday mornings. But the exact dates change every year.

items: Elephant fair (local goods market) — open every day throughout the festival, roughly 9:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., free entry, and you can walk it all day and night.
Elephant buffet (feeding the elephants) — usually held on the Friday before the show, in the morning, around the Phraya Surin Phakdi Monument, free to watch from the roadside.
Elephant arena show — Saturday and Sunday, morning sessions, roughly 8:30 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. You need a ticket, and it's the highlight you have to time carefully.
Parade and folk performances — some years held on a weekday evening, free to watch. Check the schedule each year.

blocks.title: Always check the official sources first
blocks.html: Before you hit book on a hotel or transport ticket, check that year's schedule from the Surin provincial page, TAT Surin, or local news pages like Long Surin and Surin Guide, because the actual show days set up the whole trip. If you book the wrong night and miss the show, you'll really kick yourself.

blocks.html: This plan works whether you arrive Friday evening or Saturday morning, but if you want to catch the elephant buffet too, come early on Friday. Day one is built around the free, roadside stuff: the elephant buffet and the elephant fair at night. Day two goes all-in on the arena show in the morning, then wraps up with food and souvenirs before heading home.

items: Day 1 (Friday) — watch the elephant buffet in the town center in the morning, check in and rest in the afternoon, then walk the elephant fair in the evening for a concert and Isan food.
Day 2 (Saturday) — head straight to the arena in the morning to catch the show, have lunch, grab souvenirs like Thai silk and single-clove garlic, then travel home.
Where to stay — spend one night in town, close to the arena and the elephant fair, so you can walk or take a tram to both on both days.
Getting around during the festival — the central streets get jammed, so use the free parking lots the province sets up and take a tram into the event. It's smoother than circling for a parking spot.

blocks.title: The key to this plan
blocks.html: Don't drive in and try to park near the arena yourself on show day. It's packed and the roads close in sections. Leave your car at one of the free lots the province sets up (such as the area in front of Suan Mai and points around town) and ride a free tram in. Since the arena show starts early, aim to reach the arena before 8:00 a.m. to grab a seat in a good zone.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Friday — Elephant buffet + elephant fair at night

items.activity: If you reach town early, have a light breakfast and walk over to the elephant buffet site
items.note: The buffet is usually held around the Phraya Surin Phakdi Monument, right in the town center

items.activity: Watch the elephants file in for the buffet — hundreds of them eating fruit laid out in a long line down the street
items.note: Free to watch from the roadside. Arrive early for good photo angles; it gets crowded by late morning

items.activity: Stroll around the old town, pay respects at Wat Burapharam, and photograph the monument
items.note: This temple at the heart of town is tied to Luang Pu Dun and is within walking distance of the buffet site

items.activity: Have lunch at an Isan spot in town, or the famous Vietnamese kuay jap noodles
items.note: See the restaurants in the section below

items.activity: Check in at your in-town hotel and rest a bit before the evening push
items.note: Pick a place near the arena or the walking street so it's an easy walk back late at night

items.activity: Start walking the elephant fair at Si Narong Stadium — shop for Thai silk, OTOP goods, and souvenirs
items.note: It's Surin's local goods market, open late until 9 p.m., with plenty of food

items.activity: Find some Isan food at the fair and catch the concert stage with that night's lineup
items.note: Each night has a different artist; check the lineup on the festival page ahead of time

items.activity: Walk or take a tram back to your hotel and rest up for an early start the next day
items.note: You need to be up early for the arena show tomorrow, so don't stay out too late

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Saturday — Arena elephant show + souvenirs before heading home

items.activity: Wake up early and have breakfast at the hotel or a spot near your stay
items.note: The show starts early, so leave time for travel and finding a seat

items.activity: Park at a free lot and take a tram into the arena
items.note: Avoid driving close to the arena, as roads close and traffic is heavy on show mornings

items.activity: Enter the arena, find your seat by ticket zone, and photograph the elephants before the show
items.note: Arriving early gets you a good seat in your booked zone

items.activity: Watch the elephant show — wild elephant round-up scenes, the war elephant procession, and elephants playing football
items.note: It's the biggest gathering of elephants in one place, running until around noon

items.activity: Leave the arena, ride a tram back to your car, and find lunch
items.note: Everyone leaves at once when the show ends, so allow extra time waiting for a tram

items.activity: Have lunch — Isan food or moo kratha in town — and rest up
items.note: In-town restaurants are easy to find; see the list below

items.activity: Grab souvenirs — Thai silk, single-clove garlic, jasmine rice, moo yor — before you go
items.note: Souvenir shops in town and at the elephant fair have a full range to choose from

items.activity: Set off home, or sit at a cafe to close out the trip before an evening train
items.note: The Lower Isan rail line stops at Surin station, conveniently in the town center

blocks.title: Want to catch even more? Stretch it to 3 days
blocks.html: If you come for the full Friday-to-Sunday three days, add Sunday for a trip to the Ban Ta Klang elephant village, the home base of the elephants that come to the festival, or easily swing by Sikhoraphum Sanctuary and the Ban Tha Sawang silk village. You'll get to see the real elephant-keeping way of life beyond the festival itself.

blocks.text: Where to stay during the festival

blocks.html: The elephant festival is Surin's high season: rooms fill up fast and prices climb every year, with some in-town hotels selling out months ahead. The rule of thumb is to pick a spot where you can walk to the elephant fair or easily take a tram to the arena, and if you're driving, check whether the hotel has its own parking, because in-town parking is hard to find during the festival. We've gathered places that are genuinely open and frequently reviewed for you to choose from, listed loosely rather than ranked, since the best one depends on your budget and the location you prefer.

items.name: Thong Tarin Hotel
items.blurb: A large, long-standing hotel that's a Surin institution, with a swimming pool, big rooms, breakfast, and on-site parking. It's in town within reach of the elephant fair and the food district, making it a comfortable choice for families.
items.meta: Sirirat Rd, Nai Mueang · pool + parking

items.name: Surin Majestic Hotel (The Grand)
items.blurb: A mid-range in-town hotel with clean rooms, breakfast, and parking. It's near the mall and the central district, so getting to the event is easy. Good for anyone who wants comfort without overspending.

items.name: Arena Hotel Surin
items.blurb: An in-town hotel near Robinson Surin, with fresh, clean rooms and parking. It usually runs a festival-season package each year and has a convenient location for the event, suited to couples or small groups.
items.meta: Near Robinson Surin, Mueang district · parking

items.name: MaYU Hotel Surin
items.blurb: A modern boutique hotel in town with well-designed, clean rooms and parking. It joins the festival-season packages each year and has an in-town location that's easy to reach the event from, ideal for those who like a stylish, photogenic stay.

items.name: Beelive Hotel Surin
items.blurb: A mid-size hotel near the airport, just a few minutes out of town. Its standout feature is a large parking lot that holds several hundred cars, ideal for drivers worried about parking during the festival. Clean rooms at a good price.
items.meta: Near Surin Airport · very large parking

items.name: The Wood Hotel Surin
items.blurb: A warm, three-star hotel about ten minutes from the town center, with convenient parking. It's quieter than the center, good for anyone with a car who wants to avoid the chaos of the festival streets.

items.name: The Hub Hotel Surin
items.blurb: A three-star hotel near Surin Airport with 24-hour check-in and parking. Clean rooms at a friendly price, good for budget travelers who don't mind being away from the center of the action.

items.name: Guesthouses and daily-rate stays in town
items.blurb: If the big hotels are all full, there are still small guesthouses and daily-rate apartments in the old town to book. They're cheap and within walking distance of the elephant fair, ideal for backpackers or late bookers.
items.meta: Old town, near the market · walk to the event

blocks.title: On prices and booking
blocks.html: The prices above are rough ranges. During the elephant festival, rooms go up and some places set a two-night minimum. Once you know your exact dates, book several weeks ahead, because the closer you get the pricier it is and the less is left. If the town is genuinely full, shift to an outskirts spot with parking and drive in to a free lot, then take a tram. That still works fine.

blocks.text: Festival parking: where to leave the car without the headache

blocks.html: Parking is what worries drivers most, because the central streets close in sections during the festival, traffic is heavy, and roadside parking fills up by early morning. The good news is that every year the province and the Surin Provincial Administrative Organization set up free parking lots around town, along with free shuttle trams into the arena. The easiest approach is not to fight your way in close to the arena, but to leave your car at a free lot and take a tram into the event.

items: Free lot in front of Suan Mai — the main lot the province opens every year, free to park, with shuttle trams into the event.
Lots at agencies around town — on show days the PAO and in-town agencies often open their lots for parking. Check the signs and on-site announcements that day.
Free shuttle trams — run from the lots into the arena on show days, helping you avoid traffic and skip a long walk.
If you're staying in town with parking — park at the hotel and just walk or take a tram in, so you don't have to pull the car out and circle for a spot.

blocks.title: Skip circling for parking on show day
blocks.html: The weekend days with the arena show are the most crowded for traffic. Don't count on parking near the arena gate. Go to a free provincial lot early and take a tram in — it saves a lot of time and frustration. The lots and tram routes may change each year, so check the announcements from the provincial page or the Surin PAO before you travel.

blocks.text: Elephant show tickets: how much, and how to book

blocks.html: The arena elephant show is the only activity you pay for. Tickets are split by seating zone, priced at roughly 250 THB and 350 THB per seat. The higher-priced zones are closer to the arena with better views, and some years the ticket comes with a snack set. Everything else — the elephant buffet, the parade, and the elephant fair — is free to watch and walk.

items: Ticket around 250 THB — general grandstand zone, with a full view of the show.
Ticket around 350 THB — zone closer to the arena with a better view; some years it includes a snack set.
Book online in advance through the province's ticketing system, or contact the Surin Provincial Office at 044 512 039.

blocks.title: Good zones sell out fast
blocks.html: The show runs on the weekend and it's very crowded, so the good zones go first. If you're coming specifically for the show, booking online ahead is safer than buying at the gate — and get to the arena early, since the session starts in the morning.

blocks.text: Restaurants in town worth stopping for

blocks.html: Meals in town are easy to find, focused on home-style, boldly flavored Isan food: som tam, larb, nam tok, tom saap, grilled pork neck, and the famous Vietnamese kuay jap. We've gathered spots that Surin locals actually go to and that are still open, listed loosely rather than ranked, since taste is down to personal preference.

items.name: Som Tam Phet Mani
items.blurb: A som tam shop that's been a town favorite for decades, known for nam tok pork, tom saap with pork ribs, oam with free-range chicken, and larb, all boldly flavored in true Isan style. Locals fill it up at lunch.
items.meta: Opposite Wat Sala Loi, Mueang district · open around 10:00–16:00

items.name: Mae Phim Pla Phao
items.blurb: Well-rounded Isan food — som tam, larb, nam tok, tom saap with soft bones, grilled pork neck, grilled chicken — with grilled fish as the standout dish. Good for groups ordering several things to share.
items.meta: Mulasat Sathon Rd, Nai Mueang · open around 11:00–20:00

items.name: Som Tam Je Bang
items.blurb: A som tam shop open for over twenty years, with the savory, punchy flavor locals love. Order it with grilled chicken and sticky rice for an easy lunch at a wallet-friendly price.
items.meta: Nai Mueang, Mueang Surin district · local shop, open daytime

items.name: Vietnamese kuay jap in town
items.blurb: Vietnamese kuay jap is a Surin specialty — chewy, soft noodles in a clear broth with minced pork, egg, and moo yor, eaten with patongko. A good light breakfast or lunch before the event.
items.meta: In-town area, several spots near the market

items.name: Surin-style khanom jeen nam ya
items.blurb: Khanom jeen with Surin-style nam ya — a rich curry sauce eaten with plenty of fresh vegetables. It's a filling, cheap, home-style breakfast you can find at the morning markets, good for lining your stomach before the elephant buffet.

items.name: Moo kratha in Surin town
items.blurb: The dinner where Surin locals meet up — good-value grill-and-hotpot buffets, perfect for closing out the first day after walking the festival. There are several spots scattered around town.
items.meta: Several spots around town · open evenings

items.name: Food at the elephant fair
items.blurb: The fair has a long food zone — Isan grills, fried snacks, local sweets, and street bites. You can graze your way through it in the evening, ideal for a first-night dinner while you're already in the event for a while.
items.meta: Inside the elephant fair, Si Narong Stadium · open until 9 p.m.

items.name: Cafes in town
items.blurb: Surin town has several new-wave cafes in the old town. Stop in for a coffee to rest your legs before the train home, or to duck out of the afternoon sun.

items.name: Surin souvenir and food shops
items.blurb: Before you go, stop at a souvenir shop to pick up single-clove garlic, jasmine rice, moo yor, and local sweets to take home. They make take-home food gifts that won't disappoint.
items.meta: Souvenir shops in town and near the train station

blocks.title: On restaurants during the festival
blocks.html: The elephant festival is crowded, so popular spots in town have long queues and some close early when they sell out. If you've got your heart set on a particular place, check its opening hours and days off on its page first, or fall back on the elephant fair, where there's plenty of food open late into the evening.

Surin is in Lower Isan and you can get there several ways, but during the elephant festival buses and trains are fuller than usual. Once you know your exact dates, book your transport ahead, just like the hotel.

items: Train — there's a Bangkok–Surin service every day, stopping at Surin station in the town center; you can walk or take a short ride to the event. Good if you'd rather not drive.
Bus — from Mo Chit there are several departures a day to Surin, taking about 7–8 hours.
Plane — fly into Buriram and connect by road to Surin, about 1.5 hours. It's the fastest option.
Driving — about 450 km from Bangkok, roughly 6 hours. Convenient for exploring around town afterward, though you'll need to plan for parking during the festival.

blocks.title: Coming by train is easier than you'd think
blocks.html: If your plan is mainly to see the event in town, the train drops you at Surin station in the town center, and you can walk or take a tram in from there — no parking headaches. It's ideal if you're not planning to drive on to spots outside town.

blocks.text: Add-on trips nearby if you have extra time

blocks.html: Since you've come all the way to Surin for the elephant festival, an extra day is well worth it, because around town you'll find the home base of the festival's elephants, old Khmer sanctuaries, and silk-weaving villages to drop by.

items.name: Ban Ta Klang Elephant Village
items.blurb: The home base of the elephants that come to the festival. Go to see the Kui mahouts' way of life with their elephants all year round, not just during the festival. It's in Tha Tum district, about 50–60 km from town.

items.name: Sikhoraphum Sanctuary
items.blurb: A Khmer sanctuary of five brick prangs, with apsara carvings reminiscent of Angkor Wat. The morning light is great for photos, and it's an easy stop on the way home.

items.name: Ban Tha Sawang Silk Village
items.blurb: A source of high-grade gold-brocade Thai silk, Surin's famous souvenir, which you can buy straight from the source. It's about 10 km from town and free to visit.

items: Only here for the weekend — drop the Friday elephant buffet, arrive Saturday evening, walk the elephant fair, then catch the arena show on Sunday morning instead.
Coming with kids — lean into the arena show and the elephant buffet, which kids love, and cut back on walking the fair late at night, since it's crowded and hot.
Don't want to drive — come by train, stay in town near the station, and rely on trams and walking. No parking hassle at all.
Got three days — add a day for the Ban Ta Klang elephant village or Sikhoraphum Sanctuary to see the elephant way of life beyond the festival.

blocks.text: Border situation to know before you plan

blocks.html: We'll be straight with you: the Ta Muen Thom sanctuary group and the Chong Chom market, which used to be popular spots, are not open as usual right now. They sit along the Thailand–Cambodia border, which is still affected by the border situation. The crossing is still closed and the area is under military control. So this elephant festival plan doesn't include those spots. If you see an old blog recommending Chong Chom, don't rely on it — always check the latest news on the crossing reopening first. The elephant festival in town and the rest of the province's attractions can be visited as normal.

faq.q: What dates is the Surin Elephant Festival in November, and which day should I come?
faq.a: The festival runs in mid-November every year, over about two weeks. In 2025 it ran from 15 to 26 November, and the province has set the 2026 dates at roughly 14 to 25 November. The day to come is the weekend in the middle of the festival, because Friday usually has the elephant buffet and the weekend is when the arena show runs. Before booking, double-check the actual show days on the provincial page.

faq.q: How far ahead should I book a hotel for the festival, and which area is best?
faq.a: Book several weeks ahead, since it's high season — rooms fill up fast and prices climb. In-town hotels like Thong Tarin, Arena, or MaYU are convenient for getting to the event and have parking. If the town is full, try an outskirts spot with a large lot like Beelive, then drive in to a free lot and take a tram — still convenient.

faq.q: If I drive myself, where do I park? Is parking hard to find during the festival?
faq.a: During the festival the central streets close in sections and roadside parking fills up fast. Every year the province and the Surin PAO set up free parking lots around town, such as in front of Suan Mai, with free shuttle trams into the arena. The easiest approach is to leave your car at a free lot and take a tram. Don't circle for parking near the arena on show day, as traffic is heavy. The lots may change each year, so check the announcements before you travel.

faq.q: Do I have to pay for tickets to everything at the elephant festival? How much?
faq.a: No — only the arena elephant show needs a ticket, priced at roughly 250 and 350 THB by seating zone. The zone closer to the arena costs more and some years includes a snack set. The elephant buffet, the parade, and the elephant fair are all free to watch and walk. If you're on a tight budget, the elephant buffet plus a walk through the fair already gives you the full festival atmosphere.

faq.q: Can I catch all the highlights in a 2-day, 1-night trip to the elephant festival?
faq.a: Yes, if you line up your days right. Day one, catch the elephant buffet in the morning and walk the elephant fair in the evening. Day two, head straight to the arena show in the morning, then grab souvenirs before heading home. That covers both the free stuff and the headline show. If you have an extra day, add the Ban Ta Klang elephant village, the home base of the festival's elephants.
